concepts.title: What is Probability?
concepts.contentHtml:
Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an event is to occur.

0 = impossible, 1 = certain, 0.5 = equally likely to happen or not.

For equally likely outcomes: P(event) = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes).

Roll a fair die: P(getting a 3) = 1/6. P(getting an even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

concepts.title: Combinations & Permutations
concepts.contentHtml:
Permutations: order matters. How many ways to arrange 3 books from 5? P(5,3) = 5×4×3 = 60.

Combinations: order doesn't matter. How many ways to choose 3 books from 5? C(5,3) = 60/6 = 10.

The formula: C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!) -- the binomial coefficient, written (n choose k).

These counting tools are essential for computing probabilities of complex events.

concepts.title: Independence & Conditional Probability
concepts.contentHtml:
Two events are independent if one happening doesn't affect the other. Then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Flipping two coins: P(both heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

Conditional probability P(A|B) is the probability of A given B has occurred. It narrows the sample space.

P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

concepts.title: The Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Bayes' Theorem lets you reverse conditional probabilities. If you know P(B|A), you can find P(A|B).

This is the mathematical foundation of updating beliefs with evidence.

Prior belief × Evidence = Posterior belief (normalized).

concepts.title: The Medical Test Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Classic example: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 95% accurate (both ways). You test positive. What's the probability you have the disease?

Most people guess ~95%. The actual answer: about 16%!

Why? With 1000 people: 10 have the disease (9.5 test positive). 990 don't (49.5 false positives). So 9.5/(9.5+49.5) ≈ 16%.

This is the base rate fallacy — ignoring how rare the disease is leads to wildly wrong intuitions.

concepts.title: Bayesian Thinking
concepts.contentHtml:
Bayes' theorem is not just a formula — it's a way of thinking.

Prior: Your initial belief before seeing evidence.
Likelihood: How well the evidence fits each hypothesis.
Posterior: Your updated belief after seeing evidence.

Bayesian reasoning is used in spam filters, medical diagnosis, machine learning, court cases, and scientific reasoning.

concepts.title: Discrete Distributions
concepts.contentHtml:
A probability distribution tells you how likely each possible outcome is.

Bernoulli: One trial, success or failure. (Coin flip.)

Binomial: n independent Bernoulli trials. "How many heads in 10 flips?" P(k successes) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1-p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.

Poisson: Counts rare events in a fixed interval. "How many emails per hour?" Characterized by rate λ.

concepts.title: The Normal Distribution
concepts.contentHtml:
The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the bell curve — the most important distribution in statistics.

Characterized by mean μ (center) and standard deviation σ (spread).

The 68-95-99.7 rule:
• 68% of data within 1σ of the mean
• 95% within 2σ
• 99.7% within 3σ

Heights, test scores, measurement errors, and countless natural phenomena follow this distribution.

concepts.title: Expected Value & Variance
concepts.contentHtml:
Expected value E[X] is the long-run average: what you'd get if you repeated the experiment infinitely many times.

For a die: E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. You never actually roll 3.5, but it's the average.

Variance Var(X) = E[(X - μ)²] measures spread. Standard deviation σ = √Var is in the same units as X.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
description: Why the bell curve is everywhere

concepts.title: The CLT
concepts.contentHtml:
The Central Limit Theorem is one of the most remarkable results in mathematics:

Take any distribution (dice, coins, anything). Average many independent samples. As the sample size grows, the distribution of the average approaches a normal distribution.

This works regardless of the original distribution! Uniform, exponential, Poisson — average enough samples and you get a bell curve.

concepts.title: Why the Bell Curve Appears Everywhere
concepts.contentHtml:
The CLT explains why so many things in nature follow bell curves:

Height: influenced by many genes + environment, each contributing a little → sum of many small effects → normal.

Measurement errors: many tiny random factors combine → normal.

Stock returns: many traders making decisions → approximately normal (though with fat tails in reality).

Whenever a quantity is the sum of many independent small contributions, expect a bell curve.

concepts.title: Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing
concepts.contentHtml:
The CLT enables the two pillars of statistical inference:

Confidence intervals: "The true mean is between 4.8 and 5.2 with 95% confidence." The CLT guarantees the sample mean is approximately normal, so we can compute these intervals.

Hypothesis testing: "Is this difference real or just noise?" The CLT lets us compute p-values — the probability of seeing data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.

concepts.title: MGF Definition & Uniqueness
concepts.contentHtml:
The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is M(t) = E[etX]. It is a powerful tool that uniquely determines the distribution of X (when it exists in a neighborhood of t = 0).

Why "moment generating"? Because the n-th derivative of M(t) evaluated at t = 0 gives the n-th moment: M'(0) = E[X], M''(0) = E[X²], and so on.

If two random variables have the same MGF, they have the same distribution. This makes MGFs a powerful tool for proving distributional results.

concepts.title: Computing Moments from the MGF
concepts.contentHtml:
The MGF encodes all moments of X. By expanding etX as a Taylor series: etX = 1 + tX + t²X²/2! + ..., taking expectations gives M(t) = 1 + tE[X] + t²E[X²]/2! + ...

To find E[X]: differentiate M(t) once, set t = 0. To find E[X²]: differentiate twice, set t = 0. The variance is then Var(X) = M''(0) - [M'(0)]².

A key property: if X and Y are independent, then MX+Y(t) = MX(t) · MY(t). The MGF converts sums of independent variables into products, making it ideal for proving the CLT and other limit theorems.

concepts.title: MGFs of Common Distributions
concepts.contentHtml:
Normal(μ, σ²): M(t) = exp(μt + σ²t²/2). Differentiating confirms E[X] = μ and Var(X) = σ².

Exponential(λ): M(t) = λ/(λ - t) for t < λ. Differentiating gives E[X] = 1/λ.

Poisson(λ): M(t) = exp(λ(et - 1)). This elegantly shows that the sum of independent Poisson variables is again Poisson: their MGFs multiply, and exp(λ₁(et-1)) · exp(λ₂(et-1)) = exp((λ₁+λ₂)(et-1)).

concepts.title: States & Transition Matrices
concepts.contentHtml:
A Markov chain is a sequence of random states where the probability of moving to the next state depends only on the current state, not the history. This is the Markov property (memorylessness).

The transition matrix P has entries Pij = probability of moving from state i to state j. Each row sums to 1 (it's a stochastic matrix).

For n-step transitions, the probability of going from state i to state j in exactly n steps is given by the (i,j) entry of Pn -- just raise the matrix to the n-th power!

concepts.title: Stationary Distributions & Ergodicity
concepts.contentHtml:
A stationary distribution π is a probability vector satisfying πP = π. It represents the long-run proportion of time spent in each state.

The Ergodic Theorem states that for an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain (one that can reach any state from any state, without periodic cycling), Pn converges to a matrix where every row is π.

This means no matter where you start, the chain eventually "forgets" its initial state and settles into the stationary distribution. This is one of the most powerful results in applied probability.

concepts.title: Applications of Markov Chains
concepts.contentHtml:
Google's PageRank: The web is modeled as a Markov chain where states are web pages and transitions are links. The stationary distribution ranks pages by importance -- this is how Google originally ranked search results.

Random walks: A particle moves left or right with fixed probabilities. Markov chains model diffusion, stock prices, and even board games.

MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo): By carefully designing a Markov chain whose stationary distribution matches a target distribution, we can sample from distributions that are otherwise impossible to compute. This revolutionized Bayesian statistics and is used in physics, biology, and machine learning.

concepts.title: Shannon Entropy
concepts.contentHtml:
Shannon entropy measures the average uncertainty (or information content) of a random variable: H(X) = -Σ p(x) log₂ p(x).

A fair coin has H = 1 bit (maximum uncertainty for two outcomes). A biased coin with P(H) = 0.99 has H ≈ 0.08 bits (very predictable, low entropy).

Entropy is maximized when all outcomes are equally likely, and equals zero when the outcome is certain. It quantifies how much "surprise" you should expect on average from a random source.

concepts.title: Mutual Information & KL Divergence
concepts.contentHtml:
Mutual information I(X;Y) measures how much knowing X reduces uncertainty about Y (and vice versa). I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y).

The Kullback-Leibler divergence DKL(P || Q) = Σ P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)) measures how one distribution differs from another. It is always non-negative (Gibbs' inequality) and equals zero only when P = Q.

KL divergence is not a true distance (it's asymmetric: DKL(P||Q) ≠ DKL(Q||P)), but it's fundamental in machine learning (loss functions), statistics (model selection), and physics (free energy).

concepts.title: Channel Capacity & Shannon's Theorems
concepts.contentHtml:
A communication channel is noisy: bits get flipped. Channel capacity C is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably.

Shannon's Noisy Channel Coding Theorem (1948) is astonishing: for any rate below capacity, there exist codes that achieve arbitrarily small error probability. Above capacity, reliable communication is impossible.

For a binary symmetric channel with error probability p: C = 1 - H(p) = 1 + p log₂ p + (1-p) log₂(1-p). Shannon's work founded information theory and laid the mathematical groundwork for the entire digital communications revolution.

concepts.title: Random Walks & Gambler's Ruin
concepts.contentHtml:
A random walk starts at position 0 and at each step moves +1 (with probability p) or -1 (with probability 1-p).

In 1D with a fair coin (p = 1/2), the walk is recurrent: it will return to the origin infinitely often with probability 1. The same is true in 2D. But in 3D and higher, the walk is transient -- it drifts away and may never return!

The Gambler's Ruin problem asks: starting with $k, playing a fair game, what is the probability of reaching $N before going broke? The answer is k/N. Against a house edge, ruin is almost certain for long play.

concepts.title: Brownian Motion
concepts.contentHtml:
Brownian motion (the Wiener process) W(t) is the continuous-time limit of a random walk. It is the most fundamental continuous stochastic process.

Key properties: W(0) = 0; increments W(t) - W(s) are normal with mean 0 and variance t-s; increments over non-overlapping intervals are independent; paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable (infinitely jagged at every scale).

Brownian motion was first observed physically by botanist Robert Brown (1827) watching pollen particles, and was explained mathematically by Einstein (1905) as evidence for atomic theory. Wiener gave the rigorous mathematical construction.
mathExpressions: W(t) - W(s) \sim N(0, t-s) \quad \text{for } t > s

concepts.title: Applications: Black-Scholes & Diffusion
concepts.contentHtml:
The Black-Scholes model assumes stock prices follow geometric Brownian motion: dS = μS dt + σS dW. This led to the Black-Scholes formula for option pricing, which revolutionized finance and earned Scholes and Merton the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics.

Diffusion processes model heat flow, chemical reactions, and population genetics. The diffusion equation ∂u/∂t = D ∂²u/∂x² connects probability (the density of a Brownian particle) to physics (heat conduction).

Stochastic processes bridge pure mathematics, physics, finance, and biology, making them among the most widely applied tools in modern science.
